passage: For weeks, Yamini had frozen at the bus stand in their kasba. The coaching classes were in the district town, an hour away, and every morning her chest went tight as the bus pulled in. Twice she walked home instead. Yusuf, her friend since primary school, didn't tell her to relax. "What's the smallest step you could manage?" "Maybe... just standing at the stand with you. Not getting on." So they stood there on Monday and Tuesday. On Wednesday she got on, and Yusuf rode one stop with her before getting off. In the evenings he dragged her on walks along the canal. "You sleep better after," he said. When the tightness still hadn't gone after two months, Yusuf said, "I think you should talk to the counsellor at the college. I'll come with you to ask."

qa.q: Where did Yusuf and Yamini walk in the evenings?
qa.a: Along the canal.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel every morning as the bus pulled in?
qa.a: She felt afraid; her chest went tight and she sometimes walked home instead.

qa.q: Which approach did Yusuf use that worked?
qa.a: He asked for the smallest step, stood with her and rode one stop, and encouraged evening walks for sleep.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel when the tightness still hasn't gone after two months?
qa.a: Yusuf may feel worried but hopeful that a trained counsellor can help, which is why he offers to come with Yamini to ask.

grounding: It shows a friend who does not tell someone to relax, helps her take small steps, encourages sleep and movement, and suggests a professional when anxiety lasts.

passage: In Accra, the night before the swim trials, Esther, sixteen, sat on the steps outside her building, breathing fast. "My hands won't stop shaking. What if I freeze on the block?" Her friend Gabriel sat beside her. He didn't say "just relax." He said, "That sounds awful. Tell me what's happening." He listened for a long time. Then: "One small thing. Tomorrow, just walk to the block. Only that." She did, and she swam. Over the next weeks he walked with her every evening and nagged her about sleeping by ten. When her panic kept coming back before every race, he said, "I think this needs more than me," and went with her to book an appointment with the school counsellor.

qa.q: What did Gabriel suggest as one small step?
qa.a: He suggested she just walk to the block tomorrow, only that.

qa.q: How did Gabriel seem to feel when he said "I think this needs more than me"?
qa.a: He seemed concerned and caring, honest enough to see that Esther's lasting panic needed a professional, not only a friend.

qa.q: What did Gabriel do that shows steady support?
qa.a: He listened without saying relax, helped her take one small step, encouraged walks and sleep, and helped her book the counsellor when the anxiety lasted.

qa.q: How might Esther see Gabriel after the trials?
qa.a: She may see him as a trusted friend who took her fear seriously and stayed with her.

grounding: Shows a supportive friend who listens without saying just relax, helps with one small step, encourages sleep and movement, and helps find a professional when anxiety lasts.

passage: After three weeks off sick, Kamal, fifteen, stood frozen at the school gate. "Everyone will stare. What if I've missed too much?" Bhavna, from his class, had come to meet him there. She didn't say "It's nothing, just come in." She said, "That's a lot to walk into. What would make it smaller?" They agreed on one thing: the side gate, straight to the library for first period only. They sat there together while she caught him up on history. Each evening that week she texted, "Walk done?" because he'd said walks helped him sleep. When he was still dreading every morning a fortnight later, she asked, "Can I come with you to the counsellor?" He nodded.

qa.q: Which period did Kamal first go to the library for?
qa.a: He went to the library for first period only.

qa.q: How did Bhavna seem to feel waiting at the gate with Kamal?
qa.a: She seemed calm and caring, patient enough to ask what would make it smaller instead of hurrying him.

qa.q: How did Bhavna support Kamal in a steady way?
qa.a: She listened without brushing it off, helped him take one small step, encouraged his evening walks and offered to go with him to the counsellor when the dread lasted.

qa.q: What would change if Bhavna had said "It's nothing, just come in"?
qa.a: Kamal would probably feel dismissed and more anxious, and might have turned back from the gate instead of taking a small step.

grounding: Shows a steady friend who listens without dismissing, helps one small step, encourages movement and sleep, and helps involve a counsellor when anxiety lasts.

passage:
Dear Tanvir,
Masi told me you've been lying awake worrying about the new school in Pune. I'm not going to tell you to relax. When I moved in Class 9, people kept saying that, and it only made me feel worse.
So here's one small step: next week, go and just walk around the new school gate with Masi. That's all. Look at it. Find the canteen.
Also, sleep. I know. But put the phone away by ten, and keep playing cricket in the evenings. It really helps the churning stomach.
If the worry doesn't shrink after a few weeks, tell Masi, and we'll help you find a counsellor. That's not a big scary thing. I saw one, too.
Call me anytime.
Mridul

qa.q: What small step does Mridul suggest for next week?
qa.a: To walk around the new school gate with Masi, look at it and find the canteen.

qa.q: How does Mridul feel about being told to relax?
qa.a: Mridul felt misunderstood and worse when people said it during a school move, so Mridul chooses not to say it to Tanvir.

qa.q: What makes Mridul's letter steady support?
qa.a: It avoids saying relax, suggests one small step, encourages sleep and cricket, and points to a counsellor if the worry lasts.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel reading that Mridul also saw a counsellor?
qa.a: Tanvir may feel less alone and less ashamed, seeing that getting help is normal.

grounding: Shows a supportive cousin who avoids saying just relax, suggests one small step, encourages sleep and movement, and offers help finding a counsellor if anxiety lasts.

passage:
Okay, you asked what helped Pema. I'm Suraj, her best friend since Class 3, so here's what I did.
Last term, before every test, Pema's hands shook and she'd say, "What if I blank out?" First I said, "Just relax." Big mistake. She went quiet and wouldn't talk to me for a day.
So I changed. I started just listening. I'd say, "That sounds scary. What's one thing you can do right now?" Sometimes it was just opening the textbook to one page.
We started walking round the school ground every evening. She said it helped her sleep.
But when she stopped coming to school on test days, I got worried. I asked if she'd tell her mum, and I went with her to the school counsellor. She's seeing someone properly now. I'm still her walking partner, though.

qa.q: What did Suraj say first that turned out to be a big mistake?
qa.a: "Just relax."

qa.q: How did Pema feel before tests?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid of blanking out, with her hands shaking.

qa.q: What did Suraj learn to do that helped Pema?
qa.a: Listen without saying "just relax", help her take one small step, keep evening walks for movement and sleep, and help her reach the counsellor when the worry lasted.

qa.q: If you were Pema, what might you want from a friend like Suraj?
qa.a: To be heard without being told to calm down, and to have someone steady beside you while you get proper help.

grounding: Suraj listens to Pema without saying just relax, helps her take small steps and move regularly, and helps her find professional support when the anxiety lasts.
